https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The Guardian Opinion Devolution Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK Simon Jenkins It’s something akin to a quiet earthquake: home nations jointly declaring their wish to be freed from English domination. A big move needs a big response Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.20 EDT Share M onday must have been a historical first. Never before have three of the four “nations” of the United Kingdom jointly demanded freedom to vote for its dissolution. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have lost confidence in England. They declared in Cardiff that the unionist government at Westminster is “coming to an end”. There was no such Celtic alliance against the Normans, Edward I or Cromwell. Celtic MPs have never formed a voting coalition in parliament. The Victorian Liberal party advanced “home rule for all”, but that was not independence and it got nowhere. Ireland rebelled, but it did so alone. When this eventually succeeded, Britain said good riddance, kept hold of Belfast and continued to centralise power in London. So this is serious stuff. Yet London politics this week treated the declaration as on a par with the Oxfordshire village of Piddington voting to go it alone to ward off the possibility of asylum seekers being housed nearby. The UK’s only serious geographical devolution came in 1999. It was half-hearted, mostly decentralising the running of the welfare state. But it surged the vote for Scottish and Welsh separatism and fed rather than abated the cause of independence. We can only imagine if ruling parties in Bavaria or Provence or Sicily had opted for independence from Germany, France or Italy – or if California said it had enough of Donald Trump’s US. The result would be political eruption. What does the Cardiff “memorandum of understanding” actually mean? The answer is not much in detail. There was advocacy of policy collaboration, as on childcare and economic growth. There were hints of moves towards further devolution, of the sort promised by Andy Burnham. But there was no suggestion of a new Celtic state, a British Celtica. The talks seemed to concentrate on self-determination, which Burnham had described as “ off limits ”, at least in the case of Scotland. Yet this was a man who declared self-determination for the Falklands would be defended even at the cost of tens of millions of pounds a year. The reality is that these three nations of the union have markedly different relations with England. Northern Ireland’s bipartisan government, a legacy of civil war and the Good Friday agreement, is clearly dysfunctional. As Donald Trump remarked last week , it really should advance toward Irish union. As interfaith relations slowly improve, a possible majority in favour of reunion also becomes more plausible. Support for union in Northern Ireland is now around one-third , with a majority among the young. Self-determination is not in Burnham’s gift but is written into Northern Ireland’s constitution. Observers accept that it must and will happen one day. Wales may also have a majority of its under-35s in favour of independence. But only a bare Welsh majority voted for even mild devolution in 1997 and support for independence hovers at 32% . The poor performance of the Welsh health and education services makes self-government ever more alarming, and the generosity of the London Exchequer ever more essential. Perhaps the novelty of the new Plaid Cymru government can transform things, but Welsh independence is at best a distant fantasy. This leaves Scotland . Here independence is an active issue. The population of 5.5 million puts the country in the 5-10 million band of Europe’s medium-sized states, such as Denmark, Norway, Finland, Austria and Switzerland. “Small is beautiful” appears to suit Europe’s distinctive welfare economies and keeps them ahead of their larger neighbours. Scottish unionists keep pointing to Scotland’s £25bn fiscal deficit , financed by London’s Treasury and sustaining the country’s struggling health service. But independence is a dynamic not static state. In 1922 Ireland was among the poorest countries in Europe , far behind Scotland. Its economic self-sufficiency seemed hopeless, and for some 30 years it was indeed in desperate straits. Yet by the 1990s Irish membership of the EU and the adoption of a fierce fiscal autonomy had utterly transformed it into the celebrated “Celtic Tiger”. From limping behind Scotland and other poorer European regions, Dublin raced ahead. It has become one of Europe’s richest nations per capita, albeit partly thanks to its status as a base for corporate tax avoidance. Ireland’s burst of economic vitality in the late 20th century could never have taken place had it remained an adjunct of Britain. Income per head is now ahead of Scotland’s, having once lagged far behind. It grew between 2012 and 2022 by 9% on average, against Scotland’s 1%. Whether Ireland is richer than Denmark is much debated, but the performance of an autonomous Ireland cannot be gainsaid. It is a lighthouse for the macro-economics of smallness. There is every reason why Scotland could feel held back by longstanding English dominance. Its economy, like the rest of Britain’s, has always been down the queue from London and the south-east. It has long felt cheated of its maritime oil and gas reserves. Trade has been crippled by Brexit. Unionists argue that the Barnett formula subsidy of £50bn a year is fair compensation. But Ireland’s experience suggests that dependence on foreign subsidy is a curse, not a blessing. The most glaring comparative statistic is that health outcomes in both Ireland and Denmark are now well ahead of Scotland’s . The scale of Glasgow’s drug deaths are a horror story. British loyalist though I may be, if I were a Scot I would have no hesitation. This is a real nation, and has been throughout history. Scotland has a personality and a culture recognised worldwide. Its capital, Edinburgh, is among Europe’s finest cities. Its “Silicon Glen” should be leading Europe’s AI revolution. Tourism is an obvious attraction. That the country should stumble behind its Nordic neighbours is absurd. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Scotland would have a tough transition to self-reliance, as did Ireland. But experience everywhere suggests that small autonomous democracies fare well, witness other relative newcomers such as Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and the Baltics. Their governments can concentrate on their own priorities and promote their own virtues. An independent Scotland would be bespoke. It could retain its royal figurehead and Commonwealth membership. It could even honour a “united kingdom” and the king could stay in Balmoral. Relations with other states, EU and non-EU, would be complicated, as they are at borders across the continent. That is for diplomacy to resolve. The issue is self-determination, not convenience. Burnham is the first British prime minister to appear sincere in decentralising political power. How far he understands its significance is moot. His beloved “metro mayors” are accountable regionally, not representatives of truly local loyalties. They appear as his agents, enacting his policies and enforcing his planning quotas on subordinate councils. He has shown he will stamp the Piddingtons of England into the ground. That is why Burnham should welcome any Scottish desire for “independence”. It would be the most exciting constitutional reform of the UK in centuries and one that, on current figures, would save the Treasury around £25bn a year – the cost of the Scottish fiscal deficit. It would also release the Tartan Tiger. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/far-claim.text: Jeremy Armstrong Mon, September 7, 2026 at 12:11 PM UTC 0 Ulrich Siegmund, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD)'s main candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, gestures as he addresses supporters at the AfD's election party -Credit:AFP via Getty Images A far-right party won a decisive victory in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt - and warned the rest of Europe that it was the shape of things to come. Alternative for Germany (AfD) has fallen short of the outright majority needed to govern alone. But it crucially secured 43.8% of the vote compared to the conservative CDU's 17.2%, and predicted a repeat of that success in the next two state elections. AfD state leader Ulrich Siegmund described the result as "sensational" and said the party had won a mandate to govern. Poland's centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned: "In Poland, only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD". The AfD's deputy leader in the German Parliament, Beatrix von Storch hit back, saying: "Our detractors need to wake up to what is happening in several other European states. Ulrich Siegmund, leader in the Saxony-Anhalt state election for the far-right Alternative for Germany -Credit:AFP via Getty Images • UK document is crucial but two-thirds either don't have it or it's out of date • Conor McGregor sparks uproar with Katie Taylor comments after boxing icon's final fight "The Conservative Party will disappear from the landscape, as has happened in Italy and is also happening in the UK and may happen in France with Marie Le Pen. "The Conservative Parties may stop existing because they do not realise that. People realise the issues dogging their lives. They don't care about people telling untrue stories about us." Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture. Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1m. Germany's intelligence assessed the state's AfD chapter as "right-wing extremist." Siegmund, 35, rejected that claim. Along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, he was overjoyed as exit polls revealed they were on track to score more than double the party's result in 2021. Under Pressure: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is facing questions about his leadership -Credit:AFP via Getty Images Siegmund, 35, a former salesman and marketer, has used social media to reach young voters and enjoyed a rapid rise to the top. He turned up to vote on a moped with his wife as a pillion passenger. With 880,000 followers on TikTok, he convinced 150,000 previously disillusioned 'non-voters' to support his party, despite its reputation for extremism. US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority. Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, even though the party's national leaders see it as a possibility. "If necessary there'll just be new elections, then we'd just get 50 or 55%," said Siegmund, while stating he was prepared to work with individual MPs or a party. Ulrich Siegmund takes a selfie at a press conference in Berlin -Credit:AFP via Getty Images The spotlight now falls on the left-wing populist BSW, which scraped into parliament but is set to win five seats and could help Siegmund come to power. The BSW is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas, and it has kept the door open to working with the AfD. AfD has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in Germany and its supporters believe they are on the march. Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at 77.8%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters. The head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, 93, a Holocaust survivor, said: "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more." One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia . When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war". Thorsten Frei, the CDU leader in the Bundestag, warned the result was a "turning point for our country". His boss Friedrich Merz, the chancellor, is now facing questions about his own future. His approval ratings are said to be between 13 and 16 percent; the lowest for a sitting chancellor since records began. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy7.text: Image source, International Organization for Migration Image caption, IOM workers receiving migrants near Guhere, north of the port town of Obock By Hafsa Khalil Published 11 October 2026, 13:05 BST Updated 5 hours ago At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said. The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says. The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered. "This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives." Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them. Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change. Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti. Image caption, The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families". The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added. More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics. In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's. The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month. Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen. https://www.westernpeople.ie/news/winnin.text: Fri, 02 Oct, 2026 - 09:47 Winning year for Ballina Order of Malta       Ballina Notes: daviddwane@gmail.com Ballina Order of Malta has paid tribute to its members who emerged from the National Senior First Aid Competitions with several top awards on September 19, including four first places. Their success was even sweeter because the prestigious annual 2026 national contest took place in Ballina this year, hosted by the highly-respected local ambulance corps of the Order of Malta. The activities were held across various indoor and outdoor venues around Ballina, on a day when the organisational skills of the host town were toasted by the hundreds of competitors and spectators from Ireland and abroad who took part, with the fine weather also a plus. Ballina Order of Malta, which is celebrating its 85th anniversary this year, was placed in top position in the Overall Team Award, as well as in the First Aid Responder (FAR) Team Test and Overall Team Attitude Test. The local team came joint first with Kilkenny in the Assisted Activities of Daily Living (AADL) National Cadet Team category. Adding to this impressive tally were the Ballina members who scored well in the FAR Individual and AADL tests. Irish contestants were joined by teams from Poland, Romania and Ukraine who competed in the Best International Team category, with Poland coming out on top.
